I gave them stretch assignments with safety nets, reviewed their work with explanations, and encouraged them to present their results. As they progressed, I realised they were beginning to know more than I did in some areas, so I connected them with specialists and gave them ownership of a subsystem. Eventually they became the team's go-to person for it and taught me new things. I celebrated their success publicly. The experience taught me that good mentoring is about enabling someone's growth even beyond your own level, and that mentoring is a two-way learning relationship. Looking back, the result came from acting early and keeping everyone informed. I also asked colleagues what they would do differently, which sharpened my approach for next time.
f: How did you adapt as they grew?
What did you learn from them?

q: Tell me about a time you had to correct a mistake in front of others.
cues: S — the mistake and the audience. T — your decision to speak up. A — how you corrected it and framed it. R — reaction and learning.
show: You corrected promptly and plainly, without excuses.
example: (illustrative) "S: I presented an incorrect capacity number to leadership. T: I noticed the error afterwards. A: I emailed a correction the same day, explained the cause and the revised conclusion. R: Leaders appreciated the transparency and the decision was unaffected."
a: I once presented a capacity estimate to leadership and, afterwards, realised that I had used the wrong baseline for one number, which changed a conclusion. I could have waited to see whether anyone noticed, but I corrected it that day. I sent a short message to everyone who had attended, stating clearly what the mistake was, the corrected figure and how it changed the recommendation. I explained how it happened, without excuses, and what I would do to prevent it, such as having a second person check the numbers. Leaders thanked me for the transparency, and the decision was not affected because it was caught quickly. It reinforced that credibility comes from being open about errors and fixing them promptly. What I would repeat is checking facts first, then involving the right people before acting. I also asked colleagues what they would do differently, which sharpened my approach for next time.
f: Why correct it immediately?
What did you change in your process?

q: Tell me about a time you used the error budget or SLOs to guide a prioritisation decision.
cues: S — the feature pressure and the reliability data. T — your responsibility for reliability. A — how you used SLO data to inform the decision. R — outcome.
demo: Data-informed trade-offs between reliability and features.
show: You presented budget data and proposed a clear action.
example: (illustrative) "S: The error budget for the quarter was nearly exhausted with a feature launch planned. T: I advised on whether to proceed. A: I showed the budget burn, recommended a staged rollout behind a flag and a pause on risky changes. R: The launch went well with no further budget loss."
a: With a feature launch approaching, our service had consumed most of its quarterly error budget after a couple of incidents. As the reliability lead, I was asked whether we should proceed. I presented the budget and burn rate data and our agreed policy, and rather than a flat no, I recommended a staged rollout behind a feature flag, a pause on other risky changes, and a clear rollback trigger. Product agreed since the plan protected the launch. The rollout proceeded to a small share of users first and then to everyone with monitoring in place, and caused no further budget loss. We also invested in fixing the incident causes. The approach worked because the policy was agreed in advance and I used it to enable the launch safely, not to block it. The part I value most is that we recorded the lessons so others could reuse them. I also asked colleagues what they would do differently, which sharpened my approach for next time.
f: How did you use the policy?
Why a staged rollout?

q: Tell me about a time you led a post-incident cleanup that took months and kept it on track.
cues: S — the incident and the list of follow-ups. T — you owned the closure. A — tracking, prioritising, reporting. R — completion and benefits.
show: You broke work into milestones and reported progress regularly.
example: (illustrative) "S: A major outage produced twenty follow-up actions. T: I was assigned to drive them to completion. A: I prioritised by risk reduction, assigned owners, held a biweekly review and reported to leadership. R: All critical actions closed within a quarter and a repeat outage did not occur."
a: After a major outage, the postmortem generated about twenty follow-up actions, and I was asked to drive them to completion. I grouped them by how much risk each removed, flagged five as critical, and assigned each an owner and a due date in the team's regular backlog. I held a short biweekly review to unblock owners, and sent a simple progress report to leadership. When capacity was tight, I helped negotiate time and, for two low-value items, recorded a conscious decision not to do them. All critical actions were complete within a quarter. When a similar trigger occurred months later, the new safeguards contained it with no customer impact. The sustained follow-through, not the postmortem document, delivered the value. I would handle it the same way again, because clarity and follow-through made the difference. I also asked colleagues what they would do differently, which sharpened my approach for next time.
f: How did you prioritise the actions?
How did you maintain momentum?

q: Tell me about a time you learned from a near miss that never became an incident.
cues: S — the near miss and how you noticed it. T — your decision to investigate. A — analysis and actions taken. R — improvement.
show: You treated it as a learning opportunity and fixed the systemic cause.
example: (illustrative) "S: A deployment almost wiped a production config due to a wrong environment variable. T: I caught it in review minutes before. A: I wrote a short near-miss review, added environment validation and a confirmation guard. R: The guard blocked a similar mistake months later."
a: Minutes before a deployment, I noticed in review that a variable would point the job at the production configuration instead of staging, which could have wiped important settings. We caught it, so nothing broke, and it would have been easy to move on. Instead, I wrote a short near-miss review with the timeline and contributing factors. We found that the tooling made it too easy to target the wrong environment. We added validation of the target environment, a confirmation step for production, and clearer naming. Months later, the guard stopped a colleague from making the same mistake. I learned that near misses are free lessons, and treating them seriously prevents real incidents without the cost of an outage. The outcome held up over time, which told me the approach, not luck, had worked. I also asked colleagues what they would do differently, which sharpened my approach for next time.
f: Why write up a near miss?
What guardrail did you add?
